extracted.intended_audience: humor writers, comedians, and students of comedy/joke structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating shaggy-dog stories and anti-jokes — long-winded, expectation-subverting jokes that end in an anticlimax or deliberately withheld payoff. Useful for comedians, humor writers, and analysts of joke mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the setup overlong / over-detailed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shaggy-dog stories are defined by being extremely long-winded anecdotes with extensive narration of typically irrelevant incidents. The elaboration and irrelevant detail are deliberate: they build expectation and invest the audience in the eventual payoff (or lack thereof). Examples/anti-patterns: a concise or economical setup undermines the shaggy-dog effect; verbose, digressive narration that seems pointless supports the form. Consider subtypes such as 'pointless punch' where 10 minutes of buildup lead to no payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the audience anticipate a big payoff?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the audience anticipate a big payoff?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective shaggy-dog/anti-joke structure relies on creating the impression that a significant twist or clever punchline is coming. The audience's expectations should be built up by the elaborate presentation so that withholding or undercutting that payoff creates surprise. If the narrative fails to suggest an upcoming payoff, the anticlimax will fall flat; conversely, overly telegraphed payoffs may reduce surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the punchline deliberately anticlimactic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defining move is an anticlimax: after long involved narration, the punchline is absurd, irrelevant, or flatly underwhelming. Anti-jokes explicitly subvert joke forms by refusing the expected payoff (e.g., 'Why did the chicken cross the road? To get to the other side.'). Sub-types include 'literalist punch' (a too-literal answer) and 'failed escalation' (audience expects a great twist but gets a flat statement). Anti-patterns: delivering a satisfying or clever twist rather than an anticlimax turns the piece into a conventional joke, not a shaggy dog/anti-joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the audience laugh at the form, not just content?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the audience laugh at the form, not just content?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the humor is meta-humor — the audience laughs at the convention being mocked (the time wasted, the pointless buildup) rather than only at the semantic content of the punchline. Evaluate whether reactions reflect amusement at the joke's structure and the subversion of expectations. If laughs come solely from an unexpectedly funny line rather than recognition of the form, the piece may not be functioning as a shaggy-dog/anti-joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the wasted time itself the joke?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the wasted time itself the joke?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For many successful shaggy-dog stories, the experience of being led through a long, pointless narrative is itself the comedic payoff. The long form's 'wasted time' should feel intentional and contribute to the humor: the frustration, boredom, or anticlimax becomes the source of laughter. Indicators: audience recognition that the buildup was gratuitous; laughter at the futility rather than at an insightful twist. If the audience feels merely bored or cheated rather than amused, the piece has missed its mark.
